artiest/andrew-cyrille.text:
Andrew Cyrille is an American avant-garde jazz drummer, born on 10 November 1939 in Brooklyn, New York, into a Haitian family. He began with a science degree at St. John's University, but was already playing jazz and switched to the Juilliard School. His first teachers were Willie Jones and Lenny McBrowne. They introduced him to Max Roach, but his great example became Philly Joe Jones. His first paid work was as an accompanist to the singer Nellie Lutcher, and early on he recorded with Coleman Hawkins.

The trumpeter Ted Curson introduced him to the pianist Cecil Taylor when he was eighteen. In 1965 Cyrille became a member of Taylor's group, with which he worked for fifteen years. Alongside this he built a career of his own. In 1974 he recorded the drum duet Dialogue of the Drums with Milford Graves. Records under his own name later included Junction in 1977, Nuba in 1979 and The Navigator in 1983. He also played with David Murray, Carla Bley, Marilyn Crispell and Reggie Workman, and was a member of Trio 3 with Oliver Lake.

Cyrille plays with power and elegance. He thinks like a composer and keeps an overview of the group, and his playing connects abstraction with conventional jazz and African-inflected rhythms. For the course he is above all an example of a drummer who, in free jazz, gave melody and structure to what might otherwise have seemed chaos.
artiest/andrew-cyrille.listen: Listen to Dialogue of the Drums and notice how two drummers answer one another. Try to hear where the rhythms coincide and where they diverge.

artiest/andrew-manze.text:
Andrew Manze is a British violinist and conductor, born on 14 January 1965 in Beckenham, Kent. He studied Classics at Clare College, Cambridge, and learned the violin with Simon Standage, among others, at the Royal Academy of Music. He played in the Amsterdam Baroque Orchestra under Ton Koopman. In this way he began as a specialist in early music. In 1996 he became associate director of the Academy of Ancient Music.

For the label Harmonia Mundi he recorded a great deal of Baroque music as a soloist. Well known are the Manchester Sonatas in 1995, Twelve Fantasias for Violin Solo and Gulliver Suite in the same year, Le Quattro Stagioni in 1996 and Bach's solo and double concertos in 1997. From 2003 to 2007 he was artistic director of The English Concert. Afterwards he also conducted more modern repertoire, such as the symphonies of Brahms with the Helsingborg Symphony Orchestra, of which he was chief conductor from 2006 to 2014, and Mendelssohn and Vaughan Williams. Since 2014 he has been chief conductor of the NDR Radiophilharmonie. In 2024 he became principal guest conductor of the Scottish Chamber Orchestra.

Manze writes and teaches, contributes to new editions of Mozart and Bach and regularly talks about music on radio and television. In 2011 he received the Rolf Schock Prize. He shows how historically informed performance practice found its way onto the ordinary concert platform.
artiest/andrew-manze.listen: Listen to Le Quattro Stagioni in Manze's recording and notice the raw, direct sound of his violin. Can you hear how he plays the fast passages sharply and with a dancing quality?

artiest/andrew-ridgeley.text:
Andrew Ridgeley, born on 26 January 1963 in Windlesham, Surrey, is an English musician. He became known as one half of Wham!, the duo he formed in 1981 with his school friend George Michael. Earlier they had been together with Ridgeley's brother Paul in the short-lived group The Executive. Michael sang, wrote most of the songs and played keyboards. Ridgeley co-wrote, played guitar and sang backing vocals. They recorded their demo tape in ten minutes in his living room.

With its first album, Fantastic, Wham! topped the British album chart. The second album, Make It Big, brought the breakthrough in the United States and yielded three number ones, both in the United Kingdom and in America. In April 1985 Wham! was the first Western pop group to play in China, a trip that attracted attention worldwide. The duo split up after a farewell concert, The Final, in front of 72,000 people at Wembley Stadium on 28 June 1986. Michael wanted to focus on a more adult audience.

Ridgeley then tried motor racing and acting. In 1990 his solo record Son of Albert appeared, with guitars and drums, but it sold poorly. Since then he has avoided publicity. After Michael's death in 2016 he inducted him into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2023. Ridgeley shows how a friendship between two schoolboys shaped the sound of the 1980s.
artiest/andrew-ridgeley.listen: Listen to Wake Me Up Before You Go-Go and notice the cheerful guitar part and the backing vocals. Try to hear how the song captures the energy of two friends in three minutes.

artiest/andrew-vanwyngarden.text:
Andrew VanWyngarden is an American singer, guitarist and songwriter, born on 1 February 1983 in Columbia, Missouri, and raised in Memphis, Tennessee. His father was editor-in-chief of the alternative newspaper the Memphis Flyer. As a child he heard him play The Who on an electric guitar. In seventh grade he got a Les Paul of his own. He loved Nirvana and Ween, and at secondary school made parody songs on the computer with Dan Treharne.

At Wesleyan University he studied music and met Ben Goldwasser. Together they formed MGMT, of which VanWyngarden is the singer, guitarist and one of the founders. He writes many of the lyrics. The album Oracular Spectacular from 2008 brought the band fame, partly thanks to the song Kids, which received a Grammy nomination. The band was also nominated for Best New Artist. In 2010 came the album Congratulations, and in 2023 the album Cosmic Dawn.

Besides MGMT, VanWyngarden worked with Kevin Barnes of Of Montreal in the project Blikk Fang. In 2014 he released a solo track for the surf film Spirit of Akasha, and since 2020 he has hosted a radio programme on WYXR. He is an example of a new generation of pop musicians who combine psychedelia and electronic pop.
artiest/andrew-vanwyngarden.listen: Listen to Kids by MGMT and notice the synthesizer melody that carries the whole song. Can you hear how his vocals sit on top of it almost disinterestedly?

artiest/andrzej-trzaskowski.text:
Andrzej Trzaskowski (23 March 1933 to 16 September 1998) was a Polish jazz musician, composer and musicologist. He was born in Kraków, began playing the piano at the age of four and formed his first jazz band at a young age. In 1950 he spent three months in prison on suspicion of belonging to an underground group. He then studied music history in Kraków and learned compositional techniques at the Experimental Studio of Polskie Radio. In 1957 he graduated with a thesis on Charlie Parker.

In 1956 he was named best jazz pianist and later moved to Warsaw, where he played with The Wreckers. With that group he toured the United States in 1962, performing at Newport and the Village Vanguard in New York, among other places. He wrote music for Polish films, such as Night Train from 1959. Around 1963 he moved from bop to free jazz. In the piece Synopsis he used serialism, polymetre and controlled elements of chance. In 1966 he recorded the album Seant with the trumpeter Ted Curson.

Trzaskowski later taught in the jazz department of the music school in Warsaw. In 1995 he received the Cross of Merit. He showed that jazz in the Eastern Bloc of the 1960s could acquire an experimental voice of its own. He is the father of Rafał Trzaskowski, mayor of Warsaw.
artiest/andrzej-trzaskowski.listen: Listen to a piece from Seant and notice Ted Curson's trumpet. Try to hear where the piece clearly remains jazz and where it becomes freer.

artiest/andrzej-trzaskowski-quintet.text:
Andrzej Trzaskowski was born in 1933 in Kraków. He began the piano at the age of four and formed his first jazz band at a young age. In 1950 he spent three months in prison, suspected of belonging to an underground group, and was afterwards not immediately allowed to go to university. He eventually studied music history in Kraków and learned new compositional techniques at the Polish Radio Experimental Studio. He was a pianist, composer and musicologist and from the mid-1950s was regarded as an authority on syncopated music.

In 1959 he settled in Warsaw and founded the band The Wreckers, inspired by Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie and hard bop. He himself took Horace Silver as his example. In 1960 his trio accompanied Stan Getz at the Jamboree festival. He also wrote film music, including for Night Train from 1959. In 1962 the band went to the United States and played in Washington, Newport, New Orleans and at the Village Vanguard in New York. As the first Polish jazz musicians there, they called themselves Iron Curtain Jazz. The group was afterwards called the Andrzej Trzaskowski Quintet. In 1965 the album Polish Jazz, Volume 4 appeared.

His music shows how jazz behind the Iron Curtain was not merely a copy, but formed a serious tradition of its own. He was a key figure in Polish jazz.
artiest/andrzej-trzaskowski-quintet.listen: Listen to Requiem dla Scotta LaFaro and notice the subdued, solemn atmosphere of this piece for a deceased bassist. Hear how the soloists give each other space instead of playing over one another.

artiest/andy-bell.text:
Andy Bell is an English singer and songwriter, born in 1964 and raised in Peterborough. He learned to sing in the school choir and as a teenager listened to bands such as OMD and Japan. In 1985 he was selling women's shoes and singing in a small band, The Void. Then he answered an advertisement in the newspaper: Vince Clarke was looking for a singer. Clarke had already made Depeche Mode, Yazoo and The Assembly. Bell passed the audition and together they formed Erasure.

In Erasure the two did what made the duo strong. Clarke built the electronic music, Bell gave it a face and a voice. His clear, emotional singing and his exuberant performances turned synth-pop into something warm and theatrical. The duo won, among other awards, a Brit Award for Best British Group. Bell was openly gay at a time when that was still far from a matter of course in the pop world, and became a role model for many fans.

From 2005 he also released solo albums, beginning with Electric Blue, with duets with Claudia Brücken and Jake Shears. Non-Stop (2010) followed, a series of theatre projects around the character Torsten, and Ten Crowns (2025). His voice remained tied to the danceable, melodic side of British electronic pop.
artiest/andy-bell.listen: Listen to Sometimes by Erasure. Notice the acoustic guitar that plays along between the synthesizers, and how in the chorus Andy Bell reaches up high with great feeling.

artiest/andy-kirk.text:
Andrew Dewey Kirk (28 May 1898 to 11 December 1992) was an American bandleader and saxophonist of the swing era. He was born in Newport, Kentucky, and grew up in Denver, Colorado. There he was taught by Wilberforce Whiteman, the father of Paul Whiteman. He played first in George Morrison's band and then in Terrence Holder's Dark Clouds of Joy. In 1929 he took over the leadership and named the group Clouds of Joy. He moved with the band from Dallas to Kansas City.

After the first recordings of 1929 and 1930 the group became popular as a model of the Kansas City sound. From 1936 Kirk made records for Decca. In 1938 he spent twelve weeks at the top of the chart with I Won't Tell a Soul, with the singer Pha Terrell. In 1942 Take It and Git became the first single to top the Harlem Hit Parade, the forerunner of Billboard's rhythm and blues chart. The pianist and arranger Mary Lou Williams later became a big name in jazz. Buddy Tate, Don Byas, Fats Navarro and, briefly, Charlie Parker also played in the band.

In 1948 Kirk disbanded the band. He afterwards worked in hotel management and real estate and was an officer of the Musicians' Union. His orchestra shows how swing from the Midwest sounded, with a loose rhythm section and plenty of room for soloists.
artiest/andy-kirk.listen: Listen to Take It and Git and notice the rhythm section and the solos. Try to hear how the band swings without becoming heavy.

artiest/andy-kirk-and-his-twelve-clouds-.text:
Andy Kirk and His Twelve Clouds of Joy was an American big band of the swing era, which grew out of a group from Dallas. That group was called Dark Clouds of Joy and was led by Terrence Holder. In 1929 the saxophonist and tuba player Andy Kirk took over the leadership. He renamed the band Clouds of Joy and moved with the musicians to Kansas City, Missouri. There they became a model of the Kansas City sound.

After the first recordings in 1929 and 1930, the band signed with Decca in 1936, for which it made many records until 1946. In 1938 it spent twelve weeks at the top of the chart with I Won't Tell a Soul, sung by Pha Terrell. In 1942 Take It and Git became the first single to reach number 1 on the Harlem Hit Parade, the forerunner of Billboard's rhythm and blues chart. The regular pianist and arranger was Mary Lou Williams, who later became a big name in jazz. Over the years Buddy Tate, Dick Wilson, Don Byas, Fats Navarro and, very briefly, Charlie Parker also played in the orchestra.

In 1948 Kirk disbanded the band. The orchestra stands for the swing of the Midwest, with a light, loose rhythm section and plenty of room for soloists, and it was a breeding ground for musicians who afterwards shaped bebop. For the course it is an example of a big band that was popular without belonging among the best-known names.
artiest/andy-kirk-and-his-twelve-clouds-.listen: Listen to Take It and Git and notice the interplay between the horns and the rhythm section. Try to hear where the soloists step forward and how the band supports them.

artiest/andy-kirk-en-his-twelve-clouds-o.text:
Andy Kirk and His Twelve Clouds of Joy is the name under which the American bandleader Andy Kirk, born in 1898 in Newport, Kentucky, became known. He grew up in Denver, played with George Morrison and then in Terrence Holder's Dark Clouds of Joy. When Holder left in 1929, Kirk became leader. The band moved from Dallas to Kansas City, where it became one of the best-known orchestras of the swing era.

At Decca the group made countless records from 1936 to 1946. The greatest success was I Won't Tell a Soul in 1938, sung by Pha Terrell, which spent twelve weeks at the top of the chart. Take It and Git from 1942 became the first single to reach number 1 on the Harlem Hit Parade. The pianist and arranger Mary Lou Williams gave the band its own sound, and she grew into one of the most important figures in jazz. The orchestra also included Buddy Tate, Don Byas and Fats Navarro, among others.

Kirk gave up the band in 1948 and afterwards worked in the hotel trade and real estate. His group shows how jazz from the Midwest sounded. It combined danceable swing with plenty of room for soloists and was a springboard for many later jazz greats.
artiest/andy-kirk-en-his-twelve-clouds-o.listen: Listen to I Won't Tell a Soul and notice the voice of Pha Terrell, singing high and soft above the orchestra. What are the horns doing around him?

artiest/andy-razaf.text:
Andy Razaf, born Andriamanantena Paul Razafinkarefo, was an American lyricist, born on 16 December 1895 in Washington, D.C. His father was a nephew of Queen Ranavalona III of Madagascar, his mother the daughter of the first African American consul on that island. After the French invasion of Madagascar, in which his father was killed, his mother fled to the United States. Razaf left school at sixteen, became an elevator boy in a building in Tin Pan Alley and wrote his first lyric a year later.

His most important partner was the pianist and composer Fats Waller. Together they wrote Ain't Misbehavin', Honeysuckle Rose, The Joint Is Jumpin', Keepin' Out of Mischief Now and Black and Blue. He also worked with Eubie Blake, James P. Johnson, Don Redman and others. The lyrics of In the Mood are also part of his work. He sometimes wrote the music himself too and in the late 1920s recorded records as a singer, often with ukulele, sometimes with James P. Johnson and Fletcher Henderson. As a young man he published poems in newspapers of the New Negro movement.

The Songwriters Hall of Fame list counts 215 songs by him, and one biographer arrived at more than eight hundred. In 1972 he was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. Razaf died in 1973 in North Hollywood. His lyrics, quick, playful and sometimes sharp, turned Waller's swing into a song that everyone could sing along to.
artiest/andy-razaf.listen: Listen to Honeysuckle Rose and notice the lyrics: how does the melody fit the words? Try to hear how the phrase sounds rhythmically.

artiest/andy-statman.text:
Andy Statman is an American klezmer clarinettist and bluegrass mandolinist, born in 1950 in New York and raised in Queens. He began on banjo and guitar at the age of twelve, following the example of his older brother Jimmy, and switched to the mandolin, which he briefly studied with his lifelong friend David Grisman. He also learned to play the saxophone. As a teenager he was already playing in Washington Square Park and with local string bands. His first fame came as a mandolinist, as an accompanist to David Bromberg and Russ Barenberg and in the bluegrass bands Country Cookin' and Breakfast Special.

In his search for roots music of every origin he ended up at klezmer, the traditional instrumental music of the Eastern European Jews. Through this he also found his way back to his Jewish roots. In the 1970s he learned klezmer clarinet from the great Dave Tarras, who left him some of his clarinets. Statman made Tarras's last recording and recorded albums himself that had great influence on the klezmer revival. Later he also played Hasidic melodies and mixed bluegrass, klezmer and jazz. With his trio, with the bassist Jim Whitney and the drummer Larry Eagle, he regularly plays in a synagogue in Greenwich Village.

In 2007 he was nominated for a Grammy for his version of Bill Monroe's Rawhide. In 2012 he received the National Heritage Fellowship, the highest American honour for folk art. Statman shows how traditional music from very different worlds comes together in a single musician.
artiest/andy-statman.listen: Listen to a klezmer piece by Andy Statman on clarinet and notice the sobbing, bending notes. Try to hear how the same player speaks a completely different language on the mandolin.

artiest/andy-summers.text:
Andy Summers is an English guitarist, born in 1942 in Lancashire and raised in Bournemouth. As a teenager he saw Thelonious Monk and Dizzy Gillespie play and fell under the spell of jazz guitarists such as Wes Montgomery. In the 1960s he played in London in Zoot Money's rhythm and blues band, which later became psychedelic as Dantalian's Chariot. He then played briefly in Soft Machine and in Eric Burdon's Animals. In Los Angeles he studied classical guitar and composition.

In 1977 he joined The Police, the trio with Sting and Stewart Copeland that emerged from the London punk scene. The band had worldwide hits with Roxanne, Message in a Bottle, Don't Stand So Close to Me and Every Breath You Take, until the group split up at the beginning of 1984. Summers wrote the guitar figure of Every Breath You Take and recorded it in one take with his 1961 Fender Stratocaster. His distinctive sound leaned heavily on chorus and echo effects. In this way a single guitar in a trio could still produce a full, coloured sound.

After The Police, Summers made two duo albums with Robert Fripp, I Advance Masked (1982) and Bewitched (1984), wrote film music and recorded a long series of solo records, often with jazz, such as a tribute to Thelonious Monk. He also exhibited as a photographer. In 2007 and 2008 he toured again with The Police. His playing showed that a rock guitarist can say more with clever chords and space than with fast solos.
artiest/andy-summers.listen: Listen to Every Breath You Take by The Police. Notice Andy Summers's guitar: he does not play the chords all at once, but lets the notes sound one by one in a repeating pattern that runs beneath Sting's vocals throughout the whole song.

artiest/andy-tielman.text:
Andy Tielman was born on 30 May 1936 in Makassar, on Celebes in what was then the Dutch East Indies. His father, a KNIL captain, gave his children music lessons. After the Japanese occupation Andy and his brothers and sister performed jazz standards and Indonesian music, and they even played for President Sukarno. In 1951 they turned Guitar Boogie into their first rock 'n' roll number, and afterwards they played work by Elvis Presley, Little Richard and Chuck Berry.

In 1957 the family moved to the Netherlands, first to Breda and later to The Hague. There The Tielman Brothers grew into the first Dutch rock band with international appeal. After a performance at the World Fair in Brussels they recorded Rock Little Baby of Mine in 1958, the first Dutch rock 'n' roll single. Their wild shows with acrobatic tricks were unprecedented in the Netherlands, and radio and television makers looked down on them. In Germany, and especially in Hamburg, they were acclaimed instead. George Harrison later remembered 'Andy, the Indo' from his own Hamburg days. With the rise of The Beatles their success declined.

Tielman is regarded as the godfather of indorock. He had a wide vocal range and played virtuoso guitar. Jan Akkerman, Barry Hay and Herman Brood named him as an important influence. In the late 1970s he withdrew for a time to the jungle of Kalimantan, after which he slowly returned to the stage. In 2005 he was made a knight. He died on 10 November 2011.
artiest/andy-tielman.listen: Listen to Rock Little Baby of Mine (1958) by The Tielman Brothers, the first Dutch rock 'n' roll single. Notice how the band takes over American rock 'n' roll, and the guitar, which drives the whole record.

artiest/andy-white.text:
Andy White was a Scottish session drummer. In the London studios of the early 1960s he was a professional who came to play on call: tight, reliable and used to delivering a recording quickly. That is how, in September 1962, he ended up in the EMI studio on Abbey Road, with a still unknown band from Liverpool.

The Beatles recorded their first single there, Love Me Do. The producer George Martin did not yet know what to make of the new drummer Ringo Starr and hired White to be on the safe side. As a result there are two versions of the song. On one Ringo drums, on the other White, while Ringo plays the tambourine on it. At the same session White also drummed on P.S. I Love You. The version with White later ended up on the debut album Please Please Me.

White played with The Beatles for only one afternoon, but that afternoon made him a well-known footnote in pop history. His story shows how the record industry worked at the time: the producer had the final say, and session musicians often played invisibly on records that later became world famous.
artiest/andy-white.listen: Listen to Love Me Do in the album version from Please Please Me. Notice Andy White's tight, simple drumming and hear whether you can pick out Ringo Starr's tambourine above it.

artiest/andy-williams.text:
Howard Andrew Williams (3 December 1927 to 25 September 2012) was an American singer, born in Wall Lake, Iowa. With his three older brothers he formed the vocal quartet the Williams Brothers in 1938, which performed on radio in the Midwest. In 1943 they moved to Los Angeles. In 1944 they sang on Bing Crosby's hit Swinging on a Star and they appeared in four musical films. Later he toured nightclubs as an accompanist to the singer Kay Thompson, where the group broke through in Las Vegas in 1947. Thompson also guided his first steps as a solo singer.

His solo career began in 1953. At the label Cadence, Canadian Sunset reached the top ten in 1956, and Butterfly became his only number 1 on the Billboard chart in 1957. In 1961 he signed with Columbia Records. In 1962 he sang Moon River, the title song of Breakfast at Tiffany's, at the Academy Awards ceremony, where the song won the prize for Best Original Song. From 1962 to 1971 he hosted The Andy Williams Show and made 43 albums, including The Andy Williams Christmas Album from 1964. His soft, warm voice suited the easy listening repertoire well.

Williams was above all an album artist. He sang Henry Mancini's Dear Heart and The Sweetheart Tree at the Academy Awards ceremonies of 1965 and 1966, and for twenty years performed at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas. He brought the relaxed pop sound of the 1960s into the living room.
artiest/andy-williams.listen: Listen to Moon River and notice the calm tempo and the smooth, soft singing. Can you hear how he does not force the words but lets them flow?

artiest/anestis-delias.text:
Anestis Delias (1912 to 31 July 1944) was a Greek bouzouki player, composer and rebetiko singer. He was born in Smyrna, on the coast of Anatolia, into a musical family. In 1922, at the age of ten, he fled with his pregnant mother and his little sister to Piraeus. His father stayed behind and was killed in the destruction of the city. The family settled in Drapetsona, a refugee district. As the only son he took all sorts of jobs to support his family. Around 1930 he worked in a taverna, where he got to know bouzouki players such as Markos Vamvakaris.

Around 1933, with Yiorgos Batis, Stratos Pagioumtzis and Vamvakaris, he formed the first professional rebetiko ensemble, the Famous Quartet of Piraeus, of which he was the youngest. Their recordings are carried by bouzouki and baglamas and have a distinctly oriental stamp in mode and language, brought by the Anatolian refugees. From 1935 Delias released songs under his own name, ten in all up to 1937. After that the censorship of the Metaxas regime intervened against rebetika. In 1938 his recordings stopped. He had become addicted to heroin, was exiled to the island of Ios and died in 1944, poor and weakened.

After his death he fell into oblivion for decades. Only the rebetiko revival from the 1960s brought him back. Markos Vamvakaris called him an angel in the rubbish. Delias stands for the raw urban music of the Greek refugees.
artiest/anestis-delias.listen: Listen to a recording by Delias and notice the bouzouki and the rough, untrained voice. Try to hear how the oriental scales colour Greek street music.

artiest/angela-lansbury.text:
Angela Lansbury (16 October 1925 to 11 October 2022) was a British actress and singer, born in London, the daughter of the Irish actress Moyna Macgill and the politician Edgar Lansbury. To escape the Blitz she went to the United States in 1940, where she studied drama. In 1942 she signed with MGM. Her first film roles were in Gaslight in 1944, National Velvet in 1944 and The Picture of Dorian Gray in 1945. Later she often played motherly roles on television and in film.

In 1957 she made her Broadway debut. She played major roles in the musicals Dear World, Gypsy and Sweeney Todd. In Stephen Sondheim's Sweeney Todd she played Mrs Lovett, and the 1984 recording, Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street, is among her best-known records. She also appeared in the Disney film Bedknobs and Broomsticks from 1971. In 1970 she moved to Ireland. From 1984 she became world famous as the detective Jessica Fletcher in the television series Murder, She Wrote.

Lansbury won six Tony Awards, six Golden Globes and received an Oscar for her lifetime achievement. In 2014 she was made a dame. Her work shows how the musical theatre of the twentieth century, with its acted singing, took shape in film and television.
artiest/angela-lansbury.listen: Listen to Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street and notice how Lansbury acts her role more than she sings it. Can you hear how humour and menace sit in the same line?

artiest/angelo-badalamenti.text: Angelo Badalamenti was born in Brooklyn in 1937 into an Italian-American family. He studied at the Manhattan School of Music and wrote pop songs. On Blue Velvet (1986) he had to help the actress Isabella Rossellini with her singing. This was the start of a collaboration of more than thirty years with the director David Lynch. Lynch described an atmosphere and Badalamenti improvised on the keyboard until it felt right. This is how the sound of Twin Peaks (1990) came about: slow synthesizer chords, reverberating guitar, jazzy double bass and a sad melody that suddenly blossoms. With Lynch he also wrote songs for the singer Julee Cruise. Lost Highway (1997) and Mulholland Drive (2001) carry the same dreamlike, ominous sound. He died in 2022.
artiest/angelo-badalamenti.listen: Listen to how the music almost stands still: long synthesizer chords, a slow bass line, and then suddenly a melody that swells and sinks away again.

artiest/angus-young.text:
Angus Young was born in 1955 in Glasgow, into a working-class family with eight children. In 1963 the family emigrated to Sydney. Music ran in the family: his brother George played in The Easybeats and his brother Malcolm became a guitarist. Angus had one guitar lesson from an older brother and taught himself the rest. Around 1970 he bought a second-hand Gibson SG, the model that became his trademark.

In 1973 he formed the hard rock band AC/DC with Malcolm. Angus played lead guitar, Malcolm rhythm guitar. At his sister's suggestion he performed in a school uniform, and on stage he did his own version of Chuck Berry's duck walk. With the singer Bon Scott the band made High Voltage (1975), Let There Be Rock and Highway to Hell (1979), among others. After Scott's death Brian Johnson joined, and still in 1980 Back in Black appeared, the band's greatest success. With The Razors Edge (1990), which includes Thunderstruck, AC/DC returned to the spotlight after a leaner period.

Young plays simple, hard riffs full of energy, rooted in blues and rock 'n' roll. No frills, but a sound you recognise at once. He is the only one to have remained a member of AC/DC without interruption from the start. In 2003 he was inducted with the band into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. His playing shows how a few strong guitar figures can carry an entire band.
artiest/angus-young.listen: Listen to the beginning of Thunderstruck by AC/DC. Notice the fast run of notes that Angus Young plays on a single string, and hear how the band then slowly builds until the whole song breaks loose.

artiest/anita-doth.text:
Anita Doth is actually called Anita Daniëlle Dels. She was born in Amsterdam in 1971, the daughter of a Surinamese father and a Dutch mother. She always wanted to sing and dance, but when fame still failed to arrive at nineteen, she took an administrative job with the police. In her spare time she performed with a girl rap group, the Trouble Sisters.

The rapper Ray Slijngaard asked her to sing a chorus for a demo. That demo went to the Belgian producers Jean-Paul De Coster and Phil Wilde, and so 2 Unlimited was born in 1991. The first single was Get Ready for This. Then came Twilight Zone, Workaholic, The Real Thing, Tribal Dance and No Limit, among others. Doth sang the choruses, Slijngaard rapped the verses. That was new: instrumental rave music from the clubs thus acquired two recognisable faces and a chorus to sing along to. After four albums the duo split up in 1996.

Doth then presented on TMF, worked as a DJ at Radio 538 and in 2000 released the solo album Reality. From 2009 she was back on stage with Slijngaard, first as Ray & Anita, later again as 2 Unlimited. In 2016 she left the group for good. Her clear voice is inseparably linked with the Eurodance of the early 1990s.
artiest/anita-doth.listen: Listen to No Limit by 2 Unlimited. Notice how the song is built from a hard synthesizer riff and a tight dance beat, and how Anita Doth's singing in the chorus provides the melodic counterweight to Ray Slijngaard's rap.

artiest/anita-o-day.text:
Anita O'Day, born Anita Belle Colton on 18 October 1919 in Kansas City and raised in Chicago, was an American jazz singer. She began in dance marathons and then sang in clubs in Chicago. There she met the drummer and bandleader Gene Krupa, who hired her in 1941 as the singer of his big band. With him she had hits such as Let Me Off Uptown. Later she sang with Stan Kenton's orchestra. With And Her Tears Flowed Like Wine she reached the American top five in 1944.

In the 1950s came her best-known work at Verve Records, between 1956 and 1964, with records such as Anita in 1956 and Anita Sings the Most in 1958. Her performance at the Newport Jazz Festival in 1958 brought her a great deal of attention. Heroin addiction led to a near-fatal overdose in 1966, after which she turned her life around. In 1981 her autobiography High Times Hard Times appeared. In 1985 she gave an anniversary concert at Carnegie Hall.

O'Day was known for her ability to keep up with fast arrangements and for her own way of singing. She treated her voice as an instrument and improvised like a soloist. In this way she became an influential jazz singer of the big band era.
artiest/anita-o-day.listen: Listen to Let Me Off Uptown and notice the conversation between her voice and Roy Eldridge's trumpet. Can you hear how she moves with the rhythm of the band?

artiest/anitta.text:
Anitta is the stage name of Larissa de Macedo Machado, born in 1993 in Honório Gurgel, a district of Rio de Janeiro. At the age of eight she sang in the choir of the church in her neighbourhood and received free dance lessons from a teacher who knew her mother. Her stage name comes from the character Anita in the book and television series Presença de Anita, a woman who could be sexy without being vulgar.

After her first single Meiga e Abusada from 2012 she signed with Warner Music Brazil. Her debut album Anitta came out in 2013, went straight to number one in Brazil and produced the hits Show das Poderosas and Zen. In June 2013 the video clip of Show das Poderosas became the most-viewed music video in Brazil on YouTube. Later albums are Ritmo Perfeito in 2014, Bang! in 2015 and Kisses in 2019. With Versions of Me from 2022 and the single Envolver she also broke through internationally.

Anitta combines pop, funk and reggaeton and sings in Portuguese, English and Spanish. She is one of the best-known artists in Brazil and one of the most influential artists on social media, named in the Time 100 Next. She campaigns on issues including climate and nature. Her career shows how a singer from a poor district of Rio, with a mix of Brazilian styles and a sharp sense of the internet, can be heard worldwide.
artiest/anitta.listen: Listen to Show das Poderosas and notice the solid dance rhythm and the way the vocals follow the beat. Can you hear the funk influence in the percussion?

artiest/ann-burton.text: Ann Burton, born Johanna Rafalowicz in Amsterdam, sang in clubs in the 1950s and in Germany for American soldiers. Billie Holiday was her great example, which can be heard in her slow, intimate phrasing. In 1967 she made the album Blue Burton with the trio of the pianist Louis van Dijk. Ballads & Burton (1969) followed. In the 1970s she became popular above all in Japan, where she performed a great deal and made records. She became one of the best-known Dutch jazz singers. She died in 1989.
artiest/ann-burton.listen: Hear how slowly and how close to the microphone she sings, as in a conversation.

artiest/ann-leaf.text:
Ann Leaf was an American organist who became known for the theatre organ, the great Wurlitzer organ that stood in cinemas and movie palaces in the first half of the twentieth century. Such organs could imitate an entire orchestra, with flutes, strings, trumpets and percussion, and were played by a single musician.

In the days of the silent film the organist played live to the film. He or she improvised or played from a collection of pieces and followed the images: a chase, a love scene or a storm. Orphans of the Storm from 1921 is a silent film by D. W. Griffith. It is known that such films were shown with live music. On the album The Mighty Wurlitzer: Music For Movie-Palace Organs her playing appears alongside that of other movie-palace organists.

Theatre organ music belongs to a time when the audience took it for granted that a film came with live music. The instrument had a sound of its own, full and trembling, with a vibrato that sounds almost like singing. It largely disappeared with the arrival of the sound film, but the recordings let us hear how an organist knitted image and music together.
artiest/ann-leaf.listen: Listen to Orphans of the Storm and notice the full, trembling sound of the organ. Try to imagine how a single musician replaces an entire orchestra.

artiest/ann-peebles.text:
Ann Peebles, born on 27 April 1947 in Kinloch, Missouri, is an American soul singer and songwriter. She was the seventh of eleven children and as a child sang in the choir of her father's church and in the family group The Peebles Choir. She also listened to rhythm and blues by Muddy Waters, Mary Wells and Aretha Franklin. In the 1960s she sang in clubs in St. Louis and in Oliver Sain's revue. In 1968 she sang in a club in Memphis and was offered a contract with Hi Records there.

The first records, produced by Willie Mitchell, had the typical Hi sound, with the Hi Rhythm Section and the Memphis Horns. Her first record, Walk Away, reached the rhythm and blues chart in 1969, and in 1970 Part Time Love followed. Then came Slipped, Tripped and Fell in Love, Breaking Up Somebody's Home and I'm Gonna Tear Your Playhouse Down, later a hit for Paul Young. With her husband Don Bryant she wrote I Can't Stand the Rain, which became the title of her 1974 album.

After Hi Records closed in 1979 she took a break. In 1989 she returned with Call Me. In 2014 she was inducted into the Memphis Music Hall of Fame. Her warm, smoky voice belongs to the Memphis soul of the 1970s.
artiest/ann-peebles.listen: Listen to I Can't Stand the Rain and notice the rhythm section, which sounds almost like dripping rain. Can you hear how her voice almost whispers on top of it?

artiest/anna-netrebko.text:
Anna Netrebko is a Russian operatic soprano, born on 18 September 1971 in Krasnodar into a family with Kuban Cossack roots. While studying at the St Petersburg Conservatory she worked as a cleaner at the Mariinsky Theatre. When she later auditioned, the conductor Valery Gergiev recognised her, and he became her mentor. In 1994 she made her debut on that stage as Susanna in Le nozze di Figaro. This was the start of her career at the Mariinsky, and in 1995 she made her American debut in San Francisco.

The international breakthrough came in August 2002 with Donna Anna in Don Giovanni at the Salzburger Festspiele, conducted by Nikolaus Harnoncourt. In 2002 she also made her debut at the Metropolitan Opera. Since 2003 she has recorded exclusively for Deutsche Grammophon, with records such as Opera Arias in 2003 and Sempre libera in 2004. She has sung at the Wiener Staatsoper, the Royal Opera and La Scala. At first she was known for lyric and coloratura roles, later she chose heavier Romantic parts, such as Leonora in Il trovatore.

Netrebko received several Echo Klassik awards and in 2007 appeared on the Time 100 list. In 2008 she became People's Artist of Russia. She showed that an opera star of the twenty-first century can also reach a large audience outside the opera house.
artiest/anna-netrebko.listen: Listen to an aria by Netrebko from Opera Arias and notice her warm, dark soprano. Try to hear how she lets high notes swell without forcing.

artiest/anne-dudley.text: Anne Dudley studied at the Royal College of Music and became known in the 1980s as a member of the electronic pop group Art of Noise. She then began writing film music. Her breakthrough was The Crying Game (1992), with classical orchestra and subtle synthesizers. For The Full Monty (1997) she won an Oscar for Best Comedy Score. She then worked on American History X (1998), with choir and large orchestra. For Paul Verhoeven she wrote the music for Zwartboek (2006) and Elle (2016). Dudley combines a classical orchestral training with her experience as a pop producer. She works as easily with orchestra and choir as with studio technique.
artiest/anne-dudley.listen: Notice how orchestra and choir are supplemented with subtle electronic sounds from the pop studio.

artiest/anne-sofie-von-otter.text:
Anne Sofie von Otter, born on 9 May 1955 in Stockholm, is a Swedish mezzo-soprano. Her father was a diplomat in Berlin during the Second World War, and she grew up in Bonn, London and Stockholm. She studied in Stockholm and at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama in London. From 1983 to 1985 she sang at the Basel Opera, where she made her debut as Alcina in Haydn's Orlando paladino. Covent Garden followed in 1985, La Scala in 1987 and in 1988 the Metropolitan Opera as Cherubino in Le nozze di Figaro.

Her repertoire includes song, opera, oratorio, and even rock and pop. Her recording of songs by Grieg won the Gramophone Record of the Year in 1993, the first time a song recording received that prize. In 2001 she made the album For the Stars with Elvis Costello. In 2007 she recorded music by composers who were imprisoned in the Theresienstadt ghetto, with Christian Gerhaher. Her father had tried during the war to spread information about the extermination camps. For the album Douce France she received a Grammy in 2015.

Von Otter played Leonora in the world premiere of Thomas Adès's The Exterminating Angel in 2016. She often works with the pianist Bengt Forsberg. Her work shows that a classical singer from the concert platform can also feel at home in pop and contemporary music.
artiest/anne-sofie-von-otter.listen: Listen to Dido and Aeneas or Messiah with Von Otter and notice her clear, warm mezzo. Try to hear how she makes the text sound natural.

artiest/anne-sophie-mutter.text:
Anne-Sophie Mutter is a German violinist, born on 29 June 1963 in Rheinfelden and raised in Wehr in Baden-Württemberg. Nobody at home played an instrument, but everyone loved classical music. She began the piano at the age of five, switched to the violin after a few months and at six won the national music prize. She studied with Erna Honigberger and then with Aida Stucki in Winterthur. In 1976, aged thirteen, she gave her first recital at the Lucerne Festival. The conductor Herbert von Karajan heard her and invited her to the Salzburger Pfingstfestspiele.

In 1978 she made her first record, with two Mozart violin concertos under Karajan and the Berliner Philharmoniker. In the 1980s she recorded the concertos of Brahms, Beethoven, Mendelssohn and Bruch for Deutsche Grammophon, and in 1984 The Four Seasons. In 1980 she made her debut in the United States with the New York Philharmonic. Her repertoire runs from the Baroque to the twentieth century. She also pays a great deal of attention to contemporary music, and composers such as Witold Lutosławski, Sofia Gubaidulina and Thomas Adès have written works for her.

Mutter has received many awards, including the Ernst von Siemens Music Prize in 2008 and the Polar Music Prize in 2019. In 1997 and 2008 she founded an association and a foundation to support young string players. She shows how a classical soloist in the age of the CD could reach a worldwide audience.
artiest/anne-sophie-mutter.listen: Listen to The Four Seasons in Mutter's recording and notice the contrast between the fast, fierce passages and the calm interludes. Try to hear where her violin paints the thunderstorm or the summer heat.

artiest/anneke-gronloh.text:
Anneke Grönloh was born in 1942 in Tondano on Celebes, then still the Dutch East Indies. She spent her first years of life in a Japanese camp in Fukuoka, while her father, an officer in the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army, had been interned even before she was born. After the war the family moved to the Netherlands and she grew up in Eindhoven. At school she met Peter Koelewijn, with whom she began performing at parties. In 1959 her career took off after she won a talent contest.

In the 1960s she had hit after hit, above all with Brandend zand, one of the best-selling Dutch songs of all time. In 1964 she represented the Netherlands at the Eurovision Song Contest with Jij bent mijn leven, which came tenth. That year she married Wim-Jaap van der Laan, a DJ at Radio Veronica. She began an international career and, besides popular songs, also sang kroncong numbers such as Bengawan Solo and Nina Bobo. Jazz was, by her own account, her favourite genre. Soerabaja from 1963 belongs to that Indo repertoire.

In 2000, on the strength of the sales of Brandend zand, she was named Singer of the Century in the Netherlands. She stopped because of health problems after a last performance in August 2017 and died in France in 2018. Her voice is clear and warm. She is important in the history of Dutch pop music because she brought the Indo music world to a wide public, at a time when Dutch songs still rarely reached the charts.
artiest/anneke-gronloh.listen: Listen to Brandend zand by Anneke Grönloh. Notice the simple accompaniment, the slow melody and how her voice carries the longing in the song.

artiest/anni-frid-lyngstad.text:
Anni-Frid Lyngstad, usually called Frida, was born in 1945 in a village in the north of Norway. Her mother was Norwegian, her father a German soldier. Fearing reprisals, the family left for Sweden, where Frida, after the early death of her mother, was raised by her grandmother in Torshälla. Her grandmother sang her old Norwegian songs, and that was where her love of music began.

At thirteen she was already singing in a dance orchestra, sometimes five hours a night. Later she sang jazz with a big band, with Ella Fitzgerald and Peggy Lee as her examples. In 1967 she won an EMI talent contest and was allowed to sing on Swedish television the same evening. In 1969 she met Benny Andersson at the Swedish song contest. He produced her first album, Frida (1971).

ABBA grew out of her relationship with Andersson and her friendship with Björn Ulvaeus and Agnetha Fältskog. Frida was one of the two female singers; her warm, somewhat darker voice formed a fine contrast with Fältskog's clear voice. Together they gave the ABBA hits their characteristic harmonies. After ABBA she made the English-language solo album Something's Going On (1982), and later Swedish-language records such as Djupa andetag (1996), before withdrawing from music. Her career shows how ABBA emerged from the Swedish dance band and schlager world.
artiest/anni-frid-lyngstad.listen: Listen to Fernando by ABBA, in which Frida has the lead vocal. Notice her warm, somewhat lower voice in the verses and how the other voices join in the chorus.

artiest/annie-belis.text:
Annie Bélis, born in 1951, is a French archaeologist, philologist, papyrologist and musician. She works as a research director at the French CNRS and specialises in the music of classical antiquity, ancient Greece and ancient Rome. She studied at the École normale supérieure in Sèvres from 1972 to 1975, passed the agrégation in classics in 1976 and took her doctorate at the Sorbonne. She then worked at the French School at Athens from 1982 to 1986. In 1986 she published her book on Aristoxenus of Tarentum and Aristotle.

Bélis herself plays piano, organ, flute and cello and learned them with various teachers. Her research covers music theory, such as her study of Aristoxenus's Harmonica, the reconstruction of instruments such as the Greek and Roman kithara and lyre, and the deciphering of music papyri. On a Berlin papyrus she showed that it is a paean to Apollo by Mesomedes of Crete. In 2004 she published her work on a papyrus in the Louvre, in which she recognised a version of Karkinos's Medea. In that piece Medea claims that she did not murder her children, unlike in Euripides and Seneca.

She directs the Ensemble Kérylos, which performs the reconstructed music of antiquity. In this way she brought sounds more than two thousand years old back to life.
artiest/annie-belis.listen: Listen to a recording by the Ensemble Kérylos and notice the sound of the ancient instruments, such as the lyre. Try to hear how strange and yet familiar a melody from antiquity can sound.

artiest/annie-lennox.text:
Annie Lennox was born on Christmas Day 1954 in Aberdeen, Scotland. At school she learned the flute and piano, sang in the choir and played in orchestras. She also took Dalcroze eurhythmics lessons, a method of learning music through movement. In 1971 she went to the Royal Academy of Music in London, but the classical world did not feel like hers and she did not finish her studies. From 1977 to 1980 she sang in The Tourists, her first band with Dave Stewart.

Lennox and Stewart then started Eurythmics together, a synth-pop duo named after that teaching method. With Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) from 1983 they broke through worldwide. In the video clip Lennox wore short orange hair and a suit, an image with which she played with the idea of masculine and feminine. Hits followed such as Love Is a Stranger, Here Comes the Rain Again, Would I Lie to You?, Sisters Are Doin' It for Themselves and There Must Be an Angel (Playing with My Heart). Around 1990 she went her own way.

Her solo album Diva (1992) produced Why and Walking on Broken Glass. On Medusa (1995) she sang songs by others, such as A Whiter Shade of Pale. For the film The Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King she co-wrote Into the West, which won an Oscar. Lennox has a low, soulful contralto voice and combined cool electronics with a great deal of feeling. She is also active in the fight against HIV and AIDS in Africa.
artiest/annie-lennox.listen: Listen to Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This) by Eurythmics. Notice the cool synthesizer pattern that is repeated again and again, and Annie Lennox's voice, which begins low and detached and later reaches out more powerfully.

artiest/annie-palmen.text:
Annie Palmen, in Dutch usually called Anny Palmen, was a Dutch singer. She was born on 19 August 1926 in IJmuiden, as Anna Maria Palmen. She began her career with dance orchestras around Haarlem and then sang for various radio stations. Her first hit was Ik zal je nooit meer vergeten in 1958. In 1960 she took part in the Dutch selection for the Eurovision Song Contest with Wat een geluk, but lost in a head-to-head to Rudi Carrell.

In 1963 she took part again, and this time she won. The song Geen ander went to the song contest in London, but the lyrics were completely rewritten, and so it became Een speeldoos. In 1967 she became a regular singer with the orchestra De Boertjes van Buuten in the monthly KRO television programme Mik, in which she played the role of Drika. It was a success. Records appeared such as Hoe zou het met m'n slapie gaan in 1968 and 20 super boerenhits in 1973.

After the end of Mik in 1972 Palmen disappeared from view. She died on 15 January 2000 in Beverwijk, aged 73. Her work shows how light music in the Netherlands in the 1960s consisted of a mixture of levenslied, schlager and television folklore.
artiest/annie-palmen.listen: Listen to Een speeldoos and notice the simple melody and the clear, soft voice. Can you hear how the song imitates a music box?

artiest/anouar-brahem.text:
Anouar Brahem is a Tunisian oud player and composer, born on 20 October 1957 in the Halfaouine district of the medina of Tunis. He studied the oud at the National Conservatory of Tunisia and then with the oud master Ali Sriti. In 1981 he went to Paris, where he stayed for four years and wrote music for Tunisian film and theatre. Later, back in Tunisia, he was director of the Ensemble musical de la ville de Tunis. He then toured the United States and Canada and signed with ECM Records.

At ECM he made a series of albums, including Barzakh in 1991, Conte de l'incroyable amour in 1992, Madar in 1994 with Jan Garbarek and Ustad Shaukat Hussain, Khomsa in 1995 and Thimar in 1998 with the saxophonist John Surman and the bassist Dave Holland. He also wrote the music for the film Les Silences du Palais in 1994. He usually plays in a small group, often with the Tunisian percussionist Lassad Hosni and the violinist Bechir Selmi. In 2017 Blue Maqams appeared, with Jack DeJohnette, Dave Holland and Django Bates, among others.

Brahem combines Arabic classical music, folk music and jazz. Together with Rabih Abou-Khalil and Dhafer Youssef he made the oud an important instrument in ethnic jazz. His calm, searching music shows how an instrument from the Middle East found space in the ECM world.
artiest/anouar-brahem.listen: Listen to a piece from Thimar and notice the interplay of the oud with the saxophone and the bass. Try to hear how the oud introduces a melody and the others respond to it.

artiest/anouk.text:
Anouk Teeuwe was born in 1975 in The Hague. Her mother sang in a blues band, and so she came into contact with music at an early age. Her youth was troubled: she ran away from home at fourteen and lived in children's homes for a time. At fifteen she stood on a stage for the first time, in a musicians' café in The Hague. She sang at weddings and parties and in 1994 went to the conservatoire in Rotterdam, but stopped after two years. Barry Hay and George Kooymans of Golden Earring saw her talent and wrote songs for her.

In 1997 she broke through with Nobody's Wife, a strong rock song in English that topped the Dutch chart for weeks. The debut album Together Alone was a great success. Then came Urban Solitude (1999) with R U Kiddin' Me, the hard Graduated Fool (2002), Hotel New York (2004) with Girl and Lost, and Who's Your Momma (2007), recorded with the producer Glen Ballard. In 2013 she sang Birds at the Eurovision Song Contest and reached the final, for the first time in years for the Netherlands. In 2018 she made her first Dutch-language album, Wen d'r maar aan.

Anouk is known for explosive rock songs, but also makes small, fragile songs such as Michel. She tried soul, funk, hip hop and blues. She became the most successful Dutch solo artist in the album chart and showed that a Dutch woman with English-language rock could reach the top.
artiest/anouk.listen: Listen to Nobody's Wife. Notice Anouk's raw, powerful voice and how the guitars come in heavy and loud in the chorus after the quieter verses.

artiest/anri.text:
Anri, born Eiko Kawashima in 1961 in Yamato in Kanagawa Prefecture, is a Japanese pop singer. In a career of more than forty years she became popular in the 1980s in city pop, the smooth, urban Japanese pop music of those years. Her debut single was Oribia o Kikinagara from 1978, written by Amii Ozaki.

Her breakthrough came in 1983 with the album Timely!!, with the hits Cat's Eye and Kanashimi ga Tomaranai. Cat's Eye was the first opening theme of the anime series of the same name from 1983 and entered at number one straight away. Summer Candles and Dolphin Ring also became well-known songs, even standards at Japanese weddings. In the 1980s and early 1990s her albums sold well and she gave successful tours, one of them with almost a hundred thousand visitors. In 2002 she worked with the jazz fusion guitarist Lee Ritenour, who produced her album Smooth Jam, Quiet Storm. In 2021 she made the single Watching Over You with Mariya Takeuchi, under the name Peach & Apricot.

City pop leans on supple rhythms, smooth synthesizers and soft vocals, with influences from American jazz fusion and soul. Many new artists from vaporwave and future funk have sampled her songs. As a result Anri has also found a new audience outside Japan and several albums were reissued in 2023. She now lives in Los Angeles.
artiest/anri.listen: Listen to Last Summer Whisper and notice the smooth singing over supple rhythms and synthesizers. Try to hear why this music suits a summer evening.

artiest/anthony-braxton.text: Anthony Braxton from Chicago joined the AACM in 1966. In 1969 he recorded For Alto, a double album for unaccompanied alto saxophone, the first of its kind. He named John Coltrane and Ornette Coleman among his influences, alongside composers such as Karlheinz Stockhausen and John Cage. Braxton gives his pieces no titles, but diagrams and numbers. He developed his own systems for composition and improvisation and wrote for groups from a single player to orchestras and opera. He also likes to play standards. He taught at Wesleyan University for more than twenty years. In 1994 he received a MacArthur grant.
artiest/anthony-braxton.listen: Listen to one saxophone without accompaniment: every sound is a building block.

artiest/anthony-jackson.text:
Anthony Jackson (23 June 1952 to 19 October 2025) was an American bassist, born in New York. He played piano first and began on guitar in his teens. When he switched to bass guitar, James Jamerson and Jack Casady impressed him most. He studied with Jerry Fisher, Lawrence Lucie and Pat Martino. As a studio musician he played in Billy Paul's band and at Philadelphia International Records. Paul's 1972 hit Me and Mrs. Jones was his first number 1. His bass on For the Love of Money by The O'Jays is also part of his early work.

He played in more than thirty countries and did more than three thousand studio sessions for more than five hundred albums. He became known above all as the man who developed the modern six-string bass guitar, which he himself called the contrabass guitar. In 1974 he approached builders with his idea of a bass tuned in fourths, BEADGC. Carl Thompson built the first one in 1975. Jackson felt that the bass guitar, as the lowest member of the guitar family, should have had six strings from the start. From 1982 he played almost only this bass, and the company Fodera released a signature model in 1984. His own albums include Europa Jazz in 1981, Casa Loco in 1983 and Interspirit in 2010.

Jackson died at the age of 73 on Staten Island, after developing Parkinson's disease. He showed how the bass could grow from an accompanying instrument into a full solo voice.
artiest/anthony-jackson.listen: Listen to For the Love of Money by The O'Jays and notice the bass, which carries the song. Try to hear how that line determines the groove of the whole piece.
